newsitem.title: CANADA: PolyGram film bid approved in Canada.
newsitem.headline: PolyGram film bid approved in Canada.

text.p: Industry Ministry John Manley announced on Thursday approval of PolyGram NV's application to set up a film subsidiary in Canada, over the objections of those who want to bolster Canada's cultural protectionism.

The new company, PolyGram Filmed Entertainment (PFE) Canada, will operate a fully integrated Canadian film company involving film, video and television production and distribution, a government statement said.
PolyGram NV is 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics NV.
Manley's spokesman, Bill Milliken, clarified subsequently that PolyGram had failed to win approval to be able to distribute foreign films in Canada directly rather than through intermediaries.
"They are not going to be doing (foreign) film distribution. They're going to be doing film production. They've agreed to abide by the law," Milliken told Reuters.

"The (film) policy is under review but there was no way it was going to be completed prior to the election, and PolyGram wanted to get on with business, so they said, 'OK, we'll abide by the policy, let's go.'"

Hollywood distributors that had already been operating in Canada have been allowed, under a "grandfathering policy", to continue to distribute American films after Ottawa brought in its restrictive policy.
PolyGram had sought but failed to win the same exemption, but will be allowed to set up shop to produce Canadian films.

The government statement said: "The company will comply with the government film distribution policy and has committeed to reinvest C$20 million or 20 percent of its Canadian revenues in film products in Canada over a five-year period."

"Most of this commitment will be in activities that will directly develop the Canadian film industry (investing in certified Canadian films, contributing to film festivals, distributing Canadian films abroad, etc.)," the statement added.

"PolyGram has established itself as a good corporate citizen during its 25-year history in the Canadian sound recording industry, developing award-winning artists such as Bryan Adams, Jann Arden, Shania Twain, Ashley MacIsaac and Terri Clark," Manley said. He added that he expected the new venture would provide new opportunities for jobs and growth.
The decision appeared to be a victory for Canadian Heritage Minister Sheila Copps, regarded as a "culture hawk" for her strong interest in protecting Canadian culture.
"PolyGram's plan is consistent with Canadian film distribution policy and furthers our objective which is to build a strong and health Canadian film industry," Copps said.
The separatist Bloc Quebecois, the official opposition in the Canadian Parliament, had urged the government in October to block PolyGram from distributing foreign movies in Canada.
